evidence.notes: All three builds use the same domain-appropriate composition: a ward capacity strip that doubles as a filter, a grouped triage queue and an inspector. All have no contract changes, clean axe results, no overflow and GET-only loads, and none has a critical failure. Y is the most complete on governed actions and state truthfulness: two-step impact previews, timestamped server-confirmed receipts, typed failure messages, a staleness banner and careful focus management. Its weak spot is that the ward cards stack vertically on mobile and push the queue down. Z nearly matches Y on action governance and handles mobile better (2x2 tiles), but it exposes MRNs in every queue row and groups by status only, so an overdue escalated alert sinks to the bottom. X has the best triage grouping (overdue first regardless of status) and a good mobile ward carousel. Its acknowledge action is a single click with no impact preview, and its success receipt has no timestamp. Overall Y ranks slightly ahead of X and Z, which are close to each other.

scorer_rationale.task_hierarchy: Queue is the dominant surface, split into 'Needs attention' (overdue, or open and unowned/critical/due soon) and 'Being handled', so the overdue escalated AL-2031 stays near the top. The detail pane is subordinate and has a placeholder when nothing is selected (AlertQueue.tsx, primary-1440.png).
scorer_rationale.domain_adaptation: Capacity board with 'Short N beds' / 'Needs N discharges' pressure labels and handoff 'held for' durations suit bed-flow coordination. The patient ref appears only in the detail facts, not in queue rows.
scorer_rationale.contract_preservation: No src/api or src/mock changes. /alerts and /alerts/:id are kept as nested routes. alert-row and ward-filter still exist, the original test passes unmodified, and the server ward/urgency filters are used.
scorer_rationale.interaction_state: Has skeletons, a filtered vs unfiltered empty state, an error with Retry, 404, a 'showing last loaded' notice on refresh failure, 409 'Load latest' that keeps input, 403 text and a viewer read-only notice. The success notice has no timestamp, and the partial scenario gets no distinct treatment.
scorer_rationale.responsive: No overflow at any width. At 375 the ward cards become a scroll-snap carousel and the queue comes first. Below 960 the detail replaces the queue and gets a back link. At 1024 the sticky detail pane clips the handoff history into an inner scroll.
scorer_rationale.accessibility: axe is clean: 29/29 focus-visible stops, a skip link, 44px targets, and urgency shown with a glyph plus text. The Acknowledge/Escalate switch uses role=tab without arrow-key tablist behaviour.
scorer_rationale.visual_consistency: Calm teal palette and consistent badges. Queue rows are bordered cards rather than a dense list, but they read as a queue, not a card wall.
scorer_rationale.maintainability: Small focused components, and useResource/useNow hooks that drop superseded responses. Triage thresholds are centralised in lib/ops.ts.
scorer_rationale.ai_governance: Escalate requires a target and a reason and the button names the target. Acknowledge fires in one click with no impact preview, and the receipt ('You are now the owner') has no server timestamp.

justified_patterns: ward capacity cards that double as a ward filter
inline inspector with an ownership box and handoff timeline
suspicious_patterns: ward stat cards resemble a KPI row, though each carries a task-relevant pressure label and filters the queue

strengths: attention grouping that surfaces the overdue escalated alert
409 recovery that keeps the user's input
queue and ward cards refresh after a mutation
the scroll-snap ward carousel keeps the queue high on mobile
defects: acknowledge has no impact or confirmation step
the success receipt has no timestamp
the handoff history is clipped inside the sticky pane at 1024
